analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave insurance program funded by payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill won 101 cosponsors in the House, all Democrats, but the Ways and Means Committee never held a markup or vote, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give workers up to 60 paid days per year to care for a new child, a seriously ill family member, or their own serious health condition, paying a monthly benefit between $580 and $4,000. A new Office of Paid Family and Medical Leave inside the Social Security Administration would run it, backed by a dedicated trust fund. It would be paid for with a 0.2% payroll tax on each of employers and employees and 0.4% on self-employment income. It would also make it illegal to fire or punish a worker for taking the leave, with court damages for violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people who today get no paid leave: the bill's findings state only 12% of U.S. workers had access to paid family leave and it reached just 4% of the lowest-paid workers. New parents, workers with serious health conditions, and people caring for ill or aging relatives would get partial wage replacement for up to 60 caregiving days per year, plus legal protection against being fired or demoted for taking it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid leave, especially low-wage earners

how_it_helps.text: Entitles any worker insured under Social Security disability rules, with earnings in the prior 12 months, to a monthly benefit for qualified caregiving, up to 60 days per 365-day benefit period, with monthly amounts between a $580 minimum and $4,000 maximum in the first year.

Funds the program with a dedicated 0.2% payroll tax on employees and employers and 0.4% on self-employment income, paid into a new Federal Family and Medical Leave Insurance Trust Fund, and bars any use of the Social Security trust fund for it.

Makes it unlawful to discharge or discriminate against a worker for applying for or receiving leave benefits, and lets workers sue for lost wages, liquidated damages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees.

Includes domestic partners and their children in the family covered, coordinates rather than preempts state paid-leave programs like California's and New Jersey's, and allows employers to keep more generous benefits.

The bill's own findings cite evidence that paid leave raises labor-force participation and earnings for new mothers, reduces reliance on public assistance, and that a majority of California employers reported positive or neutral effects on their businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Employers pay a 0.2% payroll tax on wages up to the Social Security wage base (about $113,700 at the time), and workers pay the same 0.2%, with self-employed people paying 0.4%. Employers also face damages liability if they retaliate against workers who take leave.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and workers, via small payroll taxes

drawbacks.text: It adds a new payroll tax of 0.2% on both employers and employees (0.4% on self-employment income) at a time when the economy was still recovering from the recession, and payroll taxes fall on every working person regardless of income below the wage cap.

Benefits are partial wage replacement capped at 60 caregiving days per year with a five-day unpaid waiting period, so workers with long illnesses or long family caregiving needs would still face unpaid time, and higher earners would see only a small share of their pay replaced.

Employers would carry new liability exposure for retaliation claims with double (liquidated) damages and attorney's fees, and would bear the administrative cost of a federal leave program layered on top of existing state and employer plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers are large and targeted at a gap that affected nearly all low-wage workers: paid time to handle birth, illness, or family care. The costs are real but modest by design — a 0.2% tax on each side of the payroll and a self-funded trust fund rather than borrowing. The main fair objections are the added tax in a weak economy, the limited 60-day cap, and the litigation exposure for employers. On balance the bill's benefits run clearly to working families; its costs are broadly shared rather than concentrated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 12, 2013 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a markup or brought it to the floor, so it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the Family and Medical Insurance Leave Act of 2013 on December 12, 2013, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
It attracted 101 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, and no Republican cosponsor.
The action history shows no further steps: no committee markup, no subcommittee action, no floor vote — the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the payroll tax and faced new leave-related liability are better off because the bill never advanced; workers without paid leave gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers spared the tax; workers gained nothing

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 12, 2013 and recruited the initial group of 39 cosigners listed on the bill text.

for.name: 101 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 101 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the committee schedule and House floor
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled committee never advanced it; the chairman's decision not to schedule a markup kept it off the floor without a recorded vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 101 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans; the bill then died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without a vote.

industries.note: Employers would pay a 0.2% payroll tax and face damages and injunctions for retaliating against workers who take leave. The bill's findings counter that most California employers reported positive or neutral effects under a similar state program, since paid leave improves retention, but the direct cost and liability run against the industry and alongside workers' gain.

A federal public benefit for the same events would partially substitute for employer-provided short-term disability coverage, though the bill explicitly coordinates with — and does not preempt — employer plans and state programs, so private plans offering richer benefits could continue alongside it.

industries.industry: State paid-family-leave programs (California, New Jersey, others)
industries.note: The bill coordinates federal benefits with state temporary disability and family leave programs and explicitly does not preempt them, keeping state programs in place and adding a federal layer on top.
